warmup.q: A topic has retention.ms set to one hour. One of its segments holds offsets 208 to 311. Offsets 208 to 249 were written two hours ago; 250 to 311 a minute ago. After the next retention check, what can a consumer still read from that segment?
options: Offsets 250 to 311: Kafka deletes each record once it is older than an hour
Offsets 208 to 311: the file stays whole until its newest record is older than an hour
Nothing: one expired record expires the whole file
Offsets 208 to 249 only: retention removes the newest records first
warmup.why: Retention deletes whole segment files, and a segment expires only when its newest record is older than retention.ms. Offsets 208 to 249 are past retention but share a file with fresh records, so they stay readable. The first option is the per-record model most people start with; the lab's broker test shows the real broker keeping exactly these records.

sections.h: One log is not enough: a topic is split into partitions
sections.html:
Lesson 1 of this track built one log: a file you only append to, where the broker numbers every record with an offset and each reader keeps one number, its position. This lesson keeps that picture and looks at how a broker actually stores it. First, though, one log for a whole topic runs into two limits.

The first limit is the reader. A consumer group keeps one position per log. Two members of the same group can't share one position: they would both read offset 50, or one would skip records the other hasn't finished. So inside a group, only one consumer reads a given log at a time. Now put numbers on it. If the fraud check needs 2 ms per payment, one consumer handles at most 500 payments a second. At a peak of 3,000 payments a second, it falls 2,500 records further behind every second.

The second limit is the machine. One log is one set of files on one broker's disk, so one broker takes every write for the topic.

Kafka's fix is to split a topic into several logs, called partitions. Each partition is a complete log of its own, exactly like the one in lesson 1: offsets start at 0, and every group has its own position in it. With 6 partitions, six fraud-check consumers in one group each read one partition, and together they handle 6 × 500 = 3,000 payments a second. Different partitions can also live on different brokers (lesson 3 of this track).

The split breaks something. One log had one order for everything. Six logs don't: offset 10 in partition 0 and offset 10 in partition 3 have no order between them. For payments that matters, because the capture of a payment must not be processed before its authorization.

The fix is the record's key. When a record has a key, the producer hashes the key and uses the hash to pick a partition, so every record with the same key lands in the same partition and stays in order there. Key payments by account id and all of one account's records keep their order, while different accounts spread across partitions. Records without a key are spread across partitions in batches. Lesson 4 of this track covers the details. The rule to remember: order is kept only within a partition.

On the broker's disk, each partition is a directory named after the topic and the partition number: card-auths-0, card-auths-1, card-auths-2. Everything about the partition lives in that directory, and nothing in it refers to another partition.

Choose the number of partitions with care. You can add partitions later but never remove them, and adding them changes which partition a key maps to. Records for one account written before the change stay in one partition, later ones may land in another, and a consumer can then see them out of order. For a payments topic keyed by account, decide the count up front.

try.title: Three partitions, three logs
steps: From the labs folder, start the broker with docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait, then open a shell in it: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka bash.
Run the commands below. They create a 3-partition topic, append six keyed card authorizations and read them back with each record's partition and offset.
Predict before you run: will six records with three keys land two per partition?
Keep the shell open for the next Try-its.

code.title: inside the kafka container
code.html: cd /opt/kafka/bin B=localhost:9092 ./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $B --create --topic card-auths --partitions 3 printf 'card-1:auth 10.00\ncard-2:auth 25.00\ncard-3:auth 7.50\ncard-1:auth 3.20\ncard-2:auth 99.00\ncard-1:auth 1.00\n' \ | ./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic card-auths \ --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=: ./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic card-auths --from-beginning --max-messages 6 \ --formatter-property print.partition=true --formatter-property print.offset=true --formatter-property print.key=true ls -d /var/lib/kafka/data/card-auths-*

try.expect:
Partition:2	Offset:0	card-1	auth 10.00
Partition:2	Offset:1	card-1	auth 3.20
Partition:2	Offset:2	card-1	auth 1.00
Partition:1	Offset:0	card-2	auth 25.00
Partition:1	Offset:1	card-3	auth 7.50
Partition:1	Offset:2	card-2	auth 99.00
/var/lib/kafka/data/card-auths-0
/var/lib/kafka/data/card-auths-1
/var/lib/kafka/data/card-auths-2

All three card-1 records are in partition 2, in the order you wrote them. card-2 and card-3 both hash to partition 1, and partition 0 got nothing: keys are hashed, not dealt out in turn. Each partition counts its own offsets from 0. The hash is deterministic, so you get the same partitions, but the two partitions may print in the other order. (The KIP-848 notice from lesson 1 prints too; it is left out here.)

sections.h: A partition is a chain of files: segments
sections.html:
A log only grows. Put numbers on that: at 3,000 payments a second of about 1 KB each, a topic takes about 3 MB a second, about 260 GB a day and about 1.8 TB a week. Sooner or later the broker must delete the oldest records.

The simplest design keeps each partition in one big file and deletes from the front. That doesn't work, because a file system can cheaply cut a file short at its end but not at its start. To drop the oldest 260 GB from a 1.8 TB file, the broker would have to copy the remaining 1.5 TB into a new file, every day.

So the broker cuts the log into a chain of files called segments. Only the newest one, the active segment, takes appends. When the active segment is full, the broker closes it and opens a new one; this is called rolling the segment. A closed segment never changes again. Deleting old data now means deleting old files, which costs almost nothing however big they are.

Each segment is named after its base offset, the offset of its first record, padded to 20 digits. The segment that starts at offset 208 is the file 00000000000000000208.log. The names solve the next problem, finding a record. To read offset 230, the broker looks for the segment with the largest base offset at or below 230. That's ...208.log. The broker keeps the segments sorted by base offset, so the lookup is quick.

Inside that file there is a second problem. A segment can be 1 GiB, and scanning it from the start at, say, 2 GB a second would take half a second for a single read. So next to each .log file sits an .index file that maps offsets to byte positions in the .log file. It is sparse: the broker adds an entry about every 4,096 bytes of data (index.interval.bytes), not one per record, which keeps the index small enough to hold in memory. The broker looks up 230 in the index, gets the byte position of the nearest entry at or below it, and reads forward a few kilobytes to offset 230. A third file, .timeindex, maps timestamps to offsets in the same sparse way, so a consumer can ask for the first record after nine o'clock.

Two topic settings decide when the active segment rolls:

Setting Default The segment rolls when
segment.bytes 1 GiB the next batch would make the file bigger than this
segment.ms 7 days the segment is older than this when a new record arrives

Kafka 4.0 raised the smallest allowed segment.bytes to 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes). To see many segments in a lab, you write large records into 1 MiB segments, which is what the Try-it below does.

try.title: Watch segments roll
steps: In the container shell, create a one-partition topic with the smallest segment size Kafka 4.4 accepts, 1 MiB.
Write 400 records of 10,000 bytes each with the bundled perf-test tool: about 4 MB.
Predict how many .log files you will see and roughly where each one starts. Then list them and print the earliest and latest offsets.

code.title: inside the kafka container, in /opt/kafka/bin
code.html: B=localhost:9092 ./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $B --create --topic ledger --partitions 1 --config segment.bytes=1048576 ./kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic ledger --num-records 400 --record-size 10000 --throughput -1 \ --command-property bootstrap.servers=$B ls -l /var/lib/kafka/data/ledger-0/ | grep '\.log' ./kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic ledger --time earliest ./kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic ledger --time latest

try.expect:
400 records sent, 1126.760563 records/sec (10.75 MB/sec), 96.03 ms avg latency, ...
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser  1047488 Nov  7 17:50 00000000000000000000.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser  1047488 Nov  7 17:50 00000000000000000104.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser  1047488 Nov  7 17:50 00000000000000000208.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser   886336 Nov  7 17:50 00000000000000000312.log
ledger:0:0
ledger:0:400

Four segments: three closed ones with 104 records each, and the active one, named 312, with the last 88. Two 10 kB records don't fit in the producer's default 16 KiB batch, so every record went in a batch of its own, about 10,072 bytes on disk. 104 of those fit in 1 MiB, and the 105th rolled the segment. The perf-test numbers depend on your machine. kafka-get-offsets.sh prints topic:partition:offset.

sections.h: Retention deletes whole segments, never single records
sections.html:
Retention decides when old data goes. A topic with cleanup.policy=delete, the default, has two limits: retention.ms (7 days by default) caps the age of the data, and retention.bytes (-1, meaning no limit, by default) caps the size of each partition.

Because the broker deletes files, not records, it needs a rule for a whole file. A segment may go only when every record in it may go. The newest record in a segment is always the last one to expire, so the rule is: a segment has expired when its newest record is older than retention.ms. Every log.retention.check.interval.ms (5 minutes by default; the lab broker uses 5 seconds), the broker walks each partition's segments from the oldest, deletes each expired one whole, and stops at the first segment that has not expired. For size, it deletes the oldest segments as long as the partition would still hold at least retention.bytes without them.

The rule has three consequences that you will meet in production.

Records live longer than retention.ms says. An old record shares its segment with newer ones and goes only when the newest has expired. On a quiet topic a 1 GiB segment may take days to fill, so it rolls on segment.ms after 7 days, and then waits until its newest record is 7 days old too. Ask for 7 days and the oldest records can stay for about 14.

The earliest offset jumps. When a segment goes, the partition's earliest offset, the oldest offset still readable, moves to the next segment's base offset: 104 records at once in the Try-it below, never one at a time. A consumer group whose committed offset now points into deleted data gets an out-of-range error on its next fetch. The consumer setting auto.offset.reset decides what happens next, and with its default, latest, the consumer jumps to the end of the partition and skips everything in between.

Deletion on disk is lazy. The broker first renames the files to .deleted and removes them a minute later (log.segment.delete.delay.ms), so that a reader still using a file can finish.

One more rule surprises people: the active segment is not protected. If every record in a partition has expired, the broker rolls a new, empty active segment and then deletes all the old ones. The partition is empty, but its offsets keep counting from where they were.

try.title: Make retention delete segments
steps: Keep the ledger topic from the previous Try-it: about 4 MB in four segments. The first block caps each partition at 2,500,000 bytes.
Predict the earliest offset after the next retention check (it runs every 5 seconds on the lab broker). Then run the first block.
The second block sets retention.ms to one second, so every record has expired. Predict the earliest and latest offsets, then run it.

00000000000000000104.log.deleted
00000000000000000208.log.deleted
00000000000000000312.log.deleted
00000000000000000400.log

The size cap removed exactly one segment, because removing the next one as well would have left the partition below 2,500,000 bytes. The earliest offset jumped from 0 to 104 in one step. With retention.ms=1000 every segment expired, the active one too, so the broker rolled a new empty segment, ...400.log, and deleted the rest. Earliest and latest are both 400: the partition is empty, and the next record will still get offset 400. The .deleted files vanish about a minute later.

sections.h: Compaction keeps the last value for each key
sections.html:
Some topics hold a current state rather than a history. Take a card-status topic: every time a card is activated, frozen or closed, a service writes a record keyed by card id. Other services read it from the beginning at start-up to build an in-memory map from card to status.

Time-based retention is wrong for this topic. A card whose status last changed three weeks ago would drop out after 7 days, and a service rebuilding its map would think the card doesn't exist. Keeping everything forever is wrong too: with 10 million cards and a few updates each per day, the topic grows without end, and a rebuild reads years of history only to keep the last line for each card.

What you want is the last record per key. That's what cleanup.policy=compact gives you. Instead of deleting old segments by age, the broker keeps at least the last record for every key and removes older records that a newer one with the same key has replaced.

A background thread on the broker, the log cleaner, does the work. It picks the partition with the largest share of not-yet-cleaned ("dirty") data, once that share passes min.cleanable.dirty.ratio (0.5 by default). It reads the dirty segments and builds a map from each key to the offset of that key's last record. Then it copies the closed segments, keeping only records whose offset is the last one for their key, and swaps the copies in.

Three rules matter to anyone who reads a compacted topic. Offsets never change: survivors keep their original offsets, so a compacted partition has gaps, and consumers skip them without noticing. Order never changes either. And the cleaner never touches the active segment, so the newest records look like a plain log until their segment rolls.

How do you delete a card, when you can only append? You append a record with the card's key and a null value, called a tombstone:

Java
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("card-status", "card-2", null));   // tombstone: card-2 is gone
Kotlin
producer.send(ProducerRecord<String, String>("card-status", "card-2", null))   // tombstone: card-2 is gone

Compaction then removes the older values for card-2. It keeps the tombstone itself for delete.retention.ms (1 day by default), because a consumer that never sees the tombstone would keep card-2 in its map forever. The clock starts when the cleaner first processes the tombstone; kafka-dump-log.sh shows the end of that window as deleteHorizonMs. A consumer that falls more than a day behind can still miss it.

Compaction is not deduplication. It keeps the last value per key only in closed segments, and only once the cleaner gets there. Until then every old value is still in the log and consumers read them all, so your code must handle every record. You can also combine both policies: cleanup.policy=compact,delete keeps the last value per key and also deletes segments past retention.

try.title: Compact a card-status topic
steps: In the container shell, create a compacted topic whose segments roll after 5 seconds, with a low dirty ratio so the cleaner starts right away.
Write six status updates that end with a tombstone for card-2. The null.marker setting turns the text NULL into a null value.
The script then waits, writes one more record to roll the first segment, and waits again so the cleaner can run. Predict which offsets survive before you read the output.
Exit the shell and stop the broker from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml down -v.

code.title: inside the kafka container, in /opt/kafka/bin
code.html: B=localhost:9092 ./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $B --create --topic card-status \ --config cleanup.policy=compact --config segment.ms=5000 --config min.cleanable.dirty.ratio=0.01 printf 'card-1:active\ncard-2:active\ncard-1:frozen\ncard-3:active\ncard-1:active\ncard-2:NULL\n' \ | ./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic card-status \ --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=: --reader-property null.marker=NULL sleep 6 # one more record: it rolls the first segment, which can now be compacted printf 'card-4:active\n' | ./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic card-status \ --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=: sleep 6 ./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic card-status --from-beginning --max-messages 4 \ --formatter-property print.offset=true --formatter-property print.key=true ./kafka-dump-log.sh --files /var/lib/kafka/data/card-status-0/00000000000000000000.log --print-data-log

try.expect:
Offset:3	card-3	active
Offset:4	card-1	active
Offset:5	card-2	null
Offset:6	card-4	active

and from the dump (trimmed):

baseOffset: 0 lastOffset: 5 count: 3 ... deleteHorizonMs: OptionalLong[1794160261750] ...
| offset: 3 ... key: card-3 payload: active
| offset: 4 ... key: card-1 payload: active
| offset: 5 ... keySize: 6 valueSize: -1 ... key: card-2

Offsets 0, 1 and 2 are gone: a later record with the same key replaced each one. The survivors kept their offsets, so the partition now starts with a gap at 0 to 2. The tombstone for card-2 is still there (valueSize: -1), and its deleteHorizonMs is one day after the cleaner first processed it. Offset 6 is in the active segment, which the cleaner never touches. If you still see all six old records, the cleaner has not run yet: wait a few seconds and read again.

analogy: Segments are the pages of the ledger book from lesson 1, and retention tears out whole pages, never single lines. A page goes only when its last line is older than the limit, so an old line at the top of a page survives as long as the page's newest line. Compaction is a different clean-up: a clerk recopies the full pages, keeps only the latest line for each account, and keeps the original line numbers so that no reference breaks. The analogy breaks on two points. The clerk never touches the page still being written, and a closed account (a tombstone) stays visible for a day before it disappears.
world: Payment topics often come with a retention rule from compliance, for example "keep authorizations for 13 months" or "never keep raw card data". Kafka's retention is a lower bound with a ragged edge: data lives until its whole segment expires, so with 1 GiB segments a quiet topic keeps records well past retention.ms. If you must delete within a day of expiry, set segment.ms low enough (say 6 hours) that segments roll often, and check the earliest offset with kafka-get-offsets.sh instead of trusting the config. Compacted topics suit reference data that your Quarkus services cache: the latest risk score per merchant, card status, currency rates. A service can rebuild its in-memory view at start-up by reading a compacted topic from the beginning, and a tombstone is how you tell every instance that a card was closed.
mistake: Assuming a lagging consumer will fail when its data has been deleted. With the default auto.offset.reset=latest, a group whose committed offset fell off the start of the log jumps to the end and carries on. Apart from one INFO line from the client about resetting the offset, nothing tells you that thousands of payments were skipped. People don't expect it because the setting sounds as if it only matters for brand-new groups. For consumers that must not skip data, set auto.offset.reset=earliest (read what is left) or none (fail loudly and let an operator decide), and alert on consumer lag long before it gets near the retention limit.

compare.title: The cleaner's offset map in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: // key -> offset of its last record; later records overwrite earlier ones Map<String, Long> last = new HashMap<>(); for (Rec r : closed) last.put(r.getKey(), r.getOffset()); List<Rec> kept = closed.stream() .filter(r -> r.getOffset() == last.get(r.getKey())) // long == Long unboxes: compares values .toList();

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: // key -> offset of its last record; associate keeps the last value for a repeated key val last: Map<String?, Long> = closed.associate { it.key to it.offset } val kept = closed.filter { it.offset == last[it.key] }

compare.note: associate builds the map in one call and keeps the last value it sees for each key, which is exactly the cleaner's rule. Java's Collectors.toMap would throw on the first repeated key unless you pass a merge function such as (a, b) -> b, so the plain loop is clearer. Watch the comparison in Java: == between two boxed Long objects compares references, which happens to work for values up to 127 and fails above. Here getOffset() returns a primitive long, so Java unboxes the other side and compares values. Kotlin's == always compares values.

worked.title: Work out what a retention change will delete before you make it

steps.say: Finance wants settlement-events kept for 3 days instead of 7. Before you change retention.ms, find out how much would go. Start with where partition 0 begins today. (admin is an Admin client; repeat for each partition.)
steps.code: // 1. where partition 0 starts today TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition("settlement-events", 0); long earliest = admin.listOffsets(Map.of(tp, OffsetSpec.earliest())) .partitionResult(tp).get().offset();

alt.html: // 1. where partition 0 starts today val tp = TopicPartition("settlement-events", 0) val earliest = admin.listOffsets(mapOf(tp to OffsetSpec.earliest())) .partitionResult(tp).get().offset()

steps.say: Find the first record younger than 3 days. OffsetSpec.forTimestamp asks the broker's time index for the earliest offset whose timestamp is at or after the time you give. If every record is older, it returns -1: everything would go.
steps.code: // 2. the first record younger than 3 days long cutoff = System.currentTimeMillis() - Duration.ofDays(3).toMillis(); long firstYoung = admin.listOffsets(Map.of(tp, OffsetSpec.forTimestamp(cutoff))) .partitionResult(tp).get().offset();

alt.html: // 2. the first record younger than 3 days val cutoff = System.currentTimeMillis() - Duration.ofDays(3).toMillis() val firstYoung = admin.listOffsets(mapOf(tp to OffsetSpec.forTimestamp(cutoff))) .partitionResult(tp).get().offset()

steps.say: Now apply the segment rule. The broker deletes only whole segments whose newest record is older than the cutoff, so the new earliest offset will be the base offset of the segment that holds firstYoung: at or below it, never above. firstYoung - earliest is the most that can go; the real number is rounded down to whole segments.
steps.code: // 3. an upper bound, rounded down to whole segments in practice System.out.printf("partition 0: up to %,d records older than 3 days%n", firstYoung - earliest);

alt.html: // 3. an upper bound, rounded down to whole segments in practice println("partition 0: up to %,d records older than 3 days".format(firstYoung - earliest))

steps.say: Change only the one key with incrementalAlterConfigs. Then watch the earliest offset over the next retention checks (every 5 minutes by default). It moves in jumps, a segment at a time.
steps.code: // 4. change retention.ms and nothing else var op = new AlterConfigOp(new ConfigEntry("retention.ms", String.valueOf(Duration.ofDays(3).toMillis())), AlterConfigOp.OpType.SET); var topic = new ConfigResource(ConfigResource.Type.TOPIC, "settlement-events"); admin.incrementalAlterConfigs(Map.of(topic, List.of(op))).all().get();

alt.html: // 4. change retention.ms and nothing else val op = AlterConfigOp(ConfigEntry("retention.ms", Duration.ofDays(3).toMillis().toString()), AlterConfigOp.OpType.SET) val topic = ConfigResource(ConfigResource.Type.TOPIC, "settlement-events") admin.incrementalAlterConfigs(mapOf(topic to listOf(op))).all().get()

lab.title: Model segments, retention and compaction, then check a real broker
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. 14 of 16 fail. The two that pass are in RetentionOnBrokerTest and need no code from you: they show a real Kafka 4.4 broker doing what your model is about to do. Offsets 0 to 249 are two hours old, retention is one hour, and the earliest offset stops at a segment boundary below 250.

In SegmentedLog.kt, write append: build the Rec, roll to a new Segment(endOffset) when the active segment already has records and this one would push it past segmentBytes, then add the record and move endOffset on.
Write deleteExpired: walk from the oldest segment, stop at the first one that has not expired, and remove the expired ones whole. If that removed every segment, add an empty one at endOffset.
Run the tests. SegmentedLogTest should pass.
In Compaction.java, write compact: one pass to find each key's last offset, a second pass to copy the survivors in order, dropping tombstones older than deleteRetentionMs.
Run the tests until all 16 pass.
hints: Roll before you append: the size check uses the record you are about to add. A segment that is still empty takes any record, however big.
A segment has expired when nowMs - maxTimestampMs > retentionMs. An empty segment's maxTimestampMs is -1, so check records.isNotEmpty() first, or an empty segment looks ancient.
In Java, Rec is a Kotlin data class: call r.getKey(), r.getValue(), r.getOffset() and r.getTimestampMs(). A HashMap<String, Long> filled in offset order leaves each key mapped to its last offset.

drill.title: Write the retention sweep from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write deleteExpired(segments, nowMs, retentionMs) for a mutable list of segments, oldest first, where each segment has records and maxTimestampMs. Delete whole expired segments from the front, stop at the first one that has not expired, and return how many you deleted. Then compare with the answer. Did you stop at the first young segment, or did you skip over it?

answer.html: static int deleteExpired(List<Segment> segments, long nowMs, long retentionMs) { int deleted = 0; while (!segments.isEmpty()) { Segment oldest = segments.get(0); boolean expired = !oldest.getRecords().isEmpty() && nowMs - oldest.getMaxTimestampMs() > retentionMs; if (!expired) break; // the first young segment stops the sweep segments.remove(0); // the whole file goes deleted++; } return deleted; }

alt.html: fun deleteExpired(segments: MutableList<Segment>, nowMs: Long, retentionMs: Long): Int { var deleted = 0 while (segments.isNotEmpty()) { val oldest = segments[0] val expired = oldest.records.isNotEmpty() && nowMs - oldest.maxTimestampMs > retentionMs if (!expired) break // the first young segment stops the sweep segments.removeAt(0) // the whole file goes deleted++ } return deleted }

recap: A topic is a set of partitions. Each partition is its own log with its own offsets, and order holds only inside one partition.
On disk a partition is a directory of segments named by base offset. Only the active segment takes appends; it rolls at segment.bytes (1 GiB) or segment.ms (7 days).
Sparse .index and .timeindex files let the broker find an offset or a timestamp without scanning the partition.
Retention deletes whole segments, oldest first, once a segment's newest record passes retention.ms or the partition is over retention.bytes. The earliest offset jumps a segment at a time.
Compaction keeps at least the last record per key in closed segments. Offsets and order never change, and tombstones stay for delete.retention.ms.

explain.prompt: A colleague set retention.ms to one hour on a test topic and is surprised that records written three hours ago are still readable. Explain why, and what they could change to see retention act sooner.
explain.answer: Retention deletes whole segment files, and a segment goes only when its newest record is older than retention.ms. On a quiet test topic the active segment keeps taking records for a long time, because the defaults are 1 GiB per segment and 7 days per segment, so the three-hour-old records share a file with newer ones. The broker also only checks every log.retention.check.interval.ms, 5 minutes by default. To see retention sooner, make the segments roll sooner: lower segment.ms on the test topic, or segment.bytes (1 MiB at least). Then old records end up in closed segments that can expire on their own.

deeper.html:
Kafka 3.9 made tiered storage production-ready (KIP-405). With remote.storage.enable=true on a topic, the broker copies closed segments to remote storage, such as an object store, through a RemoteStorageManager plugin you configure. It keeps only recent segments on local disk, as set by local.retention.ms and local.retention.bytes. Their default, -2, means "the same as retention.ms / retention.bytes", so nothing changes until you lower them. Consumers that read old offsets get the data from remote storage without knowing it. This only works because of segments: a closed segment never changes, so the broker can ship it as one file. The active segment always stays on local disk.

A few more settings are worth a look once you run compacted topics. min.compaction.lag.ms keeps recent values uncompacted for a while, so consumers see them. max.compaction.lag.ms asks the cleaner to compact a record within some time, though the design doc calls it a deadline the cleaner may miss. And kafka-log-dirs.sh --describe shows how much disk each partition uses on each broker, which is the quickest way to find the partition that retention is not keeping in check.
